source: Hansson, SEP entry: Logic of Belief Revision
finding: AGM has eight revision postulates (Closure, Success, Inclusion, Vacuity, Consistency, Extensionality plus Superexpansion and Subexpansion). Success (the new input is always accepted) is the most contested. Revision is defined as contract by the negation, then expand (Levi identity).
numbers: 6 basic + 2 supplementary revision postulates; 6 basic contraction postulates (incl. Recovery).
quote: The most controversial of them is Success.
limits: Read about 100,000 of 108,277 characters, through a summarising fetch, so wording is paraphrase. No empirical test of AGM in the entry.
agent_relevance: S5 Revise should not blindly accept the newest input: a check result is evidence, not an order. Success is the postulate to drop first.

source: Hansson, SEP entry: Recovery postulate counterexamples
finding: Recovery says contracting by p and re-adding p restores everything. Three counterexamples (Cleopatra had a child; George mass murderer vs shoplifter; Levi's coin toss) show it forces beliefs back that should stay gone. Belief-base contraction avoids it; core-retainment implies it; severe withdrawal drops it but has the odd property of Expulsiveness.
numbers: Recovery: K is a subset of (K minus p) plus p. 3 named counterexamples.
limits: A normative dispute settled by intuition, not by data.
agent_relevance: When the agent drops a candidate and later re-adds it, do not assume all that depended on it returns; keep the log of what was dropped and why.

source: Hansson, SEP entry: epistemic entrenchment
finding: An entrenchment order has five postulates: Transitivity, Dominance, Conjunctiveness, Minimality, Maximality. Rule: q survives contraction by p if q is in K and p is strictly less entrenched than p-or-q. Entrenchment-based contraction coincides exactly with transitively relational partial meet contraction.
numbers: 5 postulates; contraction rule: q in K-p iff q in K and p < (p or q), or p is a tautology.
quote: Dominance: if p entails q then p is no more entrenched than q
limits: The entry gives no procedure for getting entrenchment from data; the order is an input.
agent_relevance: Test results can supply the order: a belief that survived more independent checks ranks higher and is given up last. This is question (a) in SUBFIELDS.

source: Hansson, SEP entry: belief bases and iteration (DP1-DP4)
finding: Belief bases differ from belief sets: {p,q} and {p, p iff q} have the same closure but revise differently after input not-p. Inconsistent bases can differ; inconsistent sets cannot. Darwiche-Pearl add DP1-DP4 for iteration. The entry says opinions differ widely on which ordering shifts are adequate.
numbers: 4 DP postulates; kernel and partial-meet base contraction; Gardenfors impossibility theorem (Ramsey test vs plausible postulates, 1986-87).
limits: Silent on complexity and on psychology beyond one remark (Weisberg 2020) that people do not hold full belief and a degree of doubt at once.
agent_relevance: Keep the candidate set as a base with provenance, not as a deductively closed set; the base keeps a record of why each item is there.

source: Booth and Meyer (2006) Admissible and Restrained Revision, JAIR 26
finding: Darwiche-Pearl postulates C1-C4 are argued to rule out Boutilier's natural revision once the penultimate input must not be ignored. Admissible revision keeps C1-C4 and adds one postulate (P). It includes the Darwiche-Pearl operator, Nayak's lexicographic revision, and a new restrained revision. Restrained is the most conservative admissible operator, lexicographic the least.
numbers: C1: a more specific later input makes the earlier one redundant. C2: a contradicting later input prevails. C3: evidence entailed by later evidence is kept. C4: no input defeats itself. (P) is stronger than C3 and C4 combined.
quote: restrained revision can also be viewed as a composite operator
limits: Formal paper with toy examples (strange animal that looks red); no empirical data. Proposes but does not carry out a principled way to choose an operator per context.
agent_relevance: A menu for repeated S5 rounds: lexicographic (newest check wins fully), natural (minimal change, forgets history) or restrained (keep as much as possible). Choose by how reliable later checks are.

source: Walsh and Johnson-Laird (2009) Changing your mind, Memory and Cognition 37, 624-631 (Exp 1)
finding: Told that a fact contradicts a belief pair, people explain the clash by revising the general conditional, not the specific fact. Minimal change (change the fewest beliefs; categorical before conditional) fails as a description. Explanation, not minimality, drives revision.
numbers: Exp 1: N=20 volunteers; 17 revised the generalization more, 2 the opposite, 1 tie (binomial p<.01). Categorical revised in 30% of explanations when the clash was with both generalizations vs 15% (one of two) and 14% (single).
limits: Small samples, adults, verbal conditionals on everyday topics. One lab (the lab that proposes the explanatory theory). Needs independent replication.
agent_relevance: Real reasoners ask why the clash happened. An S5 step that asks for an explanation of the contradiction before choosing what to drop is closer to human practice than a pure minimal-change rule.

source: Walsh and Johnson-Laird (2009) Exp 2 and 3: minimalism violated
finding: When the explanation denied the categorical fact, people also rejected the consequence of a second, unrelated generalization, which minimalism says should stay. This persisted even when the consequence had been explicitly drawn before the contradiction arrived.
numbers: Exp 2: N=31 Princeton students; minimalism violated on 84% of trials (Wilcoxon z=3.62); asking for an explanation lowered rejection of the other inference, 23% vs 44%. Exp 3: N=40 Plymouth students (3 dropped); 91% violations (z=4.88); second inference rejected 51% vs accepted 15%; after a consistent fact only 1% rejected.
limits: The 2/3 chance baseline for counting a violation is the authors' choice. Student samples.
agent_relevance: Collateral damage after a revision is normal in humans too. The agent should re-check items that shared a premise with the dropped one instead of assuming they survive.

source: Walsh and Johnson-Laird (2009) Exp 4: ease of explaining moderates revision
finding: A test that separates minimalism from the explanatory account. When the contradicted rule had many known exceptions (disablers), people kept the other rule's consequence 57% of the time. With few exceptions they kept it only 21%, because they blamed the fact. Minimalism predicts no difference.
numbers: Exp 4: N=25 Princeton undergraduates in two groups; 57% vs 21% accept; Mann-Whitney U=22.5, p<.01.
limits: Between-group comparison on small groups; 12 conditional pairs.
agent_relevance: How plausible an exception is decides which belief to give up. For S5, record how many known ways each candidate could fail, and drop high-exception items first.

source: Frosch and Johnson-Laird (2006) The revision of beliefs about causes and enabling conditions, Cognitive Science Society
finding: Beliefs about causes and enabling conditions are revised differently. After consistent information most people kept their belief in the enabler but only about half kept their belief in the cause. After inconsistent information a little over half switched the enabler while most kept the cause.
numbers: Enabler, consistent trials: 88% maintained vs 12% switched to cause. Cause, consistent trials: 58% vs 42%. Enabler, inconsistent trials: 43% maintained vs 57% switched (n.s. in the text).
limits: Conference paper; N not read; some participants were replaced because they could not tell cause from enabler; one experiment.
agent_relevance: Entrenchment is not only evidence count: a belief marked as a necessary cause is held harder than a mere enabler. Tag candidate beliefs by role.

source: Elio and Pelletier (1997) Belief change as propositional update, Cognitive Science 21
finding: Original human test of whether people revise a conditional or a categorical fact on a clash. Walsh and Johnson-Laird cite it for the minimalist prediction that changing the categorical belief is the smaller change, and report that people often change the conditional instead. Not opened here.
numbers: Not read; no numbers.
limits: Second-hand through Walsh and Johnson-Laird (2009); the publisher page returned HTTP 403.
agent_relevance: Human data on revision rest on a few labs; treat as moderate evidence.

source: Wilie, Cahyawijaya et al. (2024) Belief Revision: The Adaptability of LLM Reasoning (Belief-R), EMNLP
finding: Belief-R tests whether an LLM revises a conclusion when a third premise defeats it (belief update, BU) and keeps it when the premise is irrelevant (belief maintain, BM). Models strong at basic logic fail to update; those that update more over-revise. No model passes.
numbers: About 30 LMs. Basic step at 75% or better for over 6B parameters; above 90% for instruction-tuned from 2.7B. Best BREU (mean of BU and BM) about 50%. Llama-3-70B direct prompt: BU 10.99, BM 92.09, BREU 51.54. GPT-4 Turbo direct: BU 19.65, BM 82.69, BREU 51.17. Mixtral 8x22B direct: BU 35.38, BM 36.57, BREU 35.98.
limits: Belief change triggered by one extra premise (modus ponens/tollens); zero-shot prompts; table rows read from a garbled PDF text extract.
agent_relevance: The central S5 risk is holding a conclusion when a check should overturn it. Use an explicit update-or-keep decision and score both directions with a no-change control.

source: Wilie et al. (2024) Belief-R: prompting and task moderators
finding: Chain of thought and plan-and-solve gave no real gain in revision. Modus tollens revision is harder than modus ponens. Revision on abstract mental-state effects is worse than on concrete events; models lean toward maintaining.
numbers: CoT and plan-and-solve move BREU by about 1 point on average. Plan-and-solve raised Mixtral 8x22B and Command R on BU by over 10 points but lowered Claude-3 Sonnet and GPT-4 Turbo. A distractor premise lowers basic logic accuracy on the same items.
limits: Zero-shot prompting only; no tool or verifier feedback; per-model effects mixed.
agent_relevance: Fits SCHEMA section 4b: telling the model to reason longer does not fix revision. An external signal is needed.

source: Dhanda (2026) DeltaLogic: minimal premise edits reveal belief-revision failures, ICLR 2026 workshop
finding: FOLIO and ProofWriter items become revision episodes (add support, add defeater, remove support, add irrelevant fact). Small models answer the original well but keep the old answer after the edit (inertia), flip on irrelevant edits, or hide in 'uncertain'.
numbers: 100 episodes built; 30-episode Qwen subset and 20-episode extension. Qwen3-1.7B: initial 0.667, revised 0.467, inertia 0.600. Qwen3-4B: 0.650 to 0.450, inertia 0.600. Phi-4-mini: 0.950 to 0.850, inertia 0.200, over-flip 0.100, abstain 0.350. Qwen3-0.6B abstains on 100%. Qwen3-1.7B gets support-insertion right but fails support-removal and defeating-fact edits.
limits: Workshop paper, n of 20-30, models of 0.6B to 4B only, log-likelihood label scoring, single author. Shows the failure mode, not a ranking.
agent_relevance: Retraction (support lost, defeater arrives) is the hard direction; adding support is easy. Treat 'remove a dependency' as its own case with its own test.

source: Jenkins (2026) AGM-Bench: do LLMs revise beliefs rationally? ICLR 2026 workshop
finding: Benchmark of the six classic AGM postulates plus Darwiche-Pearl iteration. Seven frontier models satisfy Success and Consistency at high rates but break Inclusion (minimal change) and Preservation (unrelated beliefs stay). Under repeated revision they show inertia (keep retracted information) and collateral damage (drop unaffected beliefs). Reasoning-trained models (o3-mini, DeepSeek-R1) improve in one step but degrade faster over iterations.
numbers: 2,400 synthetic scenarios, 7 models, 6 AGM postulates plus DP postulates. Per-postulate rates not available.
limits: Only the abstract page was read, through a summarising fetch; the full paper and its numbers were not opened; workshop paper, one author.
agent_relevance: The two failures to guard in repeated S5 rounds are inertia and collateral loss. Log both per round.

source: Hase, Hofweber et al. (2024) Fundamental problems with model editing: how should rational belief revision work in LLMs?
finding: Frames model editing as belief revision, lists 12 open problems, and builds a Wikidata-based testbed where an ideal Bayesian agent gives the correct updated beliefs. A small LM trained from scratch learns the facts, but after a rank-one edit it does not update the downstream facts.
numbers: 83M-parameter LM, 1B tokens (5 epochs); memorises over 90% of 100k true facts. For edits that should change a downstream answer, downstream accuracy goes 0.97 before to 0.01 after. Probabilistic error (MAE) on the edited fact falls 0.23 to 0.05 but on the downstream fact rises 0.34 to 0.59. Logical-coherence errors for 'and' and 'or' sentences stay about 0.34 and 0.22.
quote: model editing is essentially belief revision
limits: Toy semi-synthetic world, small model, one rank-one editing method; real LLMs may differ. AGM assumes logical omniscience, which LLMs lack.
agent_relevance: Never assume that stating a correction updates what depends on it. After S5 changes a belief, derived beliefs must be recomputed or re-checked.

source: Cohen et al. (2023) Evaluating the ripple effects of knowledge editing in language models (RippleEdits)
finding: 5K factual edits with ripple tests (logical generalisation, compositionality, subject aliasing, preservation). ROME, MEMIT and MEND succeed on the edited fact and on aliasing but miss implied facts. A simple in-context editing baseline (put the new fact in the prompt) scores best.
numbers: Subject aliasing 86.8 or higher in all settings. Logical Generalization for ROME on GPT-J: 53.8 on random facts vs 5.5 on popular facts. In-context editing beats ROME by over 10 points on GPT-Neo and 29 points on LLaMA on average; GPT-3 with in-context editing is best overall.
limits: GPT-2 to GPT-3 and LLaMA-7B era models; popularity of the edited entity changes results a lot.
agent_relevance: Putting the revised belief and its consequences in context beats changing stored weights. This supports a scaffold-level revision (rewrite the working belief set).

source: Zhong et al. (2023) MQuAKE: assessing knowledge editing via multi-hop questions, EMNLP
finding: Edited models recall the new fact but fail multi-hop questions that need it. A memory method (MeLLo) stores edits outside the model and checks each tentative sub-answer against them; it does far better, and better with stronger base models.
numbers: GPT-J, MQuAKE-CF: ROME edit-wise 88.3, MEMIT 96.2, yet multi-hop accuracy after edit is single digits to about 20 against 40.5 unedited (table text partly garbled). MeLLo with GPT-3.5 over 1 to 4 edits: 52.1, 35.3, 31.8, 30.9 on CF; 91.1, 87.4, 86.2, 85.5 on MQuAKE-T. MEMIT on GPT-J: 11.8 to 5.4 over 1 to 4 edits (CF); MeLLo on GPT-J: 38.9 to 14.2.
limits: Up to 4 edits per case; Wikidata facts; accuracy drops as edits accumulate even for MeLLo.
agent_relevance: MeLLo's loop (answer, check the sub-answer against a stored edit list, override on conflict) is a working small-scale S5. It still decays with more edits, so cap and prune the list.

source: Xie et al. (2024) Adaptive chameleon or stubborn sloth: LLM behaviour in knowledge conflicts, ICLR
finding: Shown coherent counter-evidence alone, LLMs mostly accept it. Shown both their own memory and counter-evidence, they favour their own (confirmation bias), more strongly for popular facts, and are sensitive to evidence order and head-count.
numbers: GPT-4: about 80% memorization ratio on the most popular questions. Order effects over 5 points for all models except GPT-4; PaLM2 and Llama2-7B over 30 points (PopQA, Llama2-7B: 33.3 with memory first vs 82.8 with counter-memory first). Share of sources: ChatGPT keeps its memory answer 30.0% at 1 of 3 sources vs 86.2% at 2 of 3 (PopQA); GPT-4 50.3% vs 91.0%.
limits: Entity-substitution counter-evidence is incoherent and is resisted (earlier work read this as stubbornness); generated counter-evidence is accepted. 8 models, 2 datasets.
agent_relevance: Entrenchment in a model is set by prior knowledge, popularity, order and head-count, not by evidence quality. S5 must score evidence by source and test, and fix or randomise order.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet, ICLR
finding: With a correctness label from outside the loop, revision helps; without it, self-correction lowers accuracy. The model changes correct answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: Oracle label: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0; GPT-4 95.5 to 97.5, 82.0 to 85.5, 49.0 to 59.0. Intrinsic, 5 calls: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 74.7, CSQA 41.8, HotpotQA 25.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 89.0, CSQA 80.0, HotpotQA 43.0. GPT-3.5 keeps its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: Prompts from earlier papers; HotpotQA only 100 questions; GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2. The oracle result is not a usable procedure.
agent_relevance: Revision needs a real signal from a test or tool. Without it, 'revise' is a noisy flip. The check must be external.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location, Findings of ACL
finding: Separates finding the mistake from correcting it. Finding is poor (best 52.87 for GPT-4 on the dataset). Correction given the true step works. A small classifier trained on other tasks locates mistakes better than prompting a large model.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2,186 CoT traces over 5 tasks. Backtracking with true location: gains on wrong traces +18.0 to +43.9 points, losses on right traces 0 to -11.4. With random location: gains +5.2 to +21.6, losses -6.7 to -15.9.
limits: Backtracking by resampling the step; few correct traces in the data; oracle location is not available in practice.
agent_relevance: Which belief to give up is the hard part, as in AGM: choosing what to retract, not the rewrite. Spend effort on locating the faulty item with a targeted test.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When can LLMs actually correct their own mistakes? A critical survey, TACL
finding: Survey of self-correction work. No prior work shows success with feedback from prompted LLMs, except on tasks unusually suited to it. Self-correction works with reliable external feedback. Large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Many studies over-evaluate through unfair set-ups.
numbers: Three conclusions; no pooled effect size.
limits: A review of mixed studies; some tasks (style, code with tests) differ from reasoning.
agent_relevance: Agrees with the schema position: use test or tool feedback for revision, not self-judgement.

source: Laban et al. (2024) Are you sure? Challenging LLMs leads to performance drops: the FlipFlop experiment
finding: After an answer, challenge with 'Are you sure?'. Ten LLMs flip often and get worse. Fine-tuning on synthetic FlipFlop dialogues cuts the damage.
numbers: 10 LLMs, 7 classification tasks: flip 46% of answers on average; accuracy falls 17% on average; seven models lose 10 or more points. Fine-tuned Mistral-7B: FlipFlop effect 9.5% down to 3.8% (60% reduction).
limits: Short-answer classification; fine-tuning shown on one open model; a bare challenge carries no new evidence.
agent_relevance: A challenge without new evidence should not cause revision. S5 should require a failing check or a new fact to flip, and log 'revised without evidence' as a defect.

source: Rios-Garcia et al. (2026) AI scientists produce results without reasoning scientifically
finding: Over 25,000 agent runs in eight domains. Agents seldom revise beliefs after refutation. The base model, not the scaffold, explains most of the behaviour.
numbers: Base model explains 41.4% of variance, scaffold 1.5%. Evidence ignored in 68% of traces; beliefs never updated in 71%; refutation-driven revision in 26%; convergent multi-test evidence 7%; untested claims 53%. Giving near-complete successful traces as context helps only a little.
limits: Reasoning graphs annotated by a pipeline built with expert labels; preprint. Per-model rows (revision 0.17, 0.07, 0.04 for three models) were read from messy text and do not obviously match the 26% overall.
agent_relevance: A scaffold alone does not produce revision. S5 needs a hard trigger: a refuting result forces a named revision step, and the run log checks that it happened.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2026) FalsifyBench: rule-discovery games from the Wason 2-4-6 task
finding: 12 LLMs play a Wason-style hidden-rule game. Models that test to falsify their hypothesis win; models that seek confirmation lose. Reasoning models beat instruction-tuned ones but none is near optimal.
numbers: 100 games per model. Success: GPT-5.2-Chat 75%, GPT-OSS-120B 68%, best instruction-tuned DeepSeek-V3.1 41%, other instruction-tuned 33-35%, GPT-5-Nano 12%, Qwen3.5-9B 21%. Confirmation bias predicts failure (posterior mean -4.15, odds ratio 0.016). Oracle errors had no credible effect. In failed games, partial-overlap hypotheses +27.0 points for GPT-5.2-Chat; surface-word hypotheses in 97.6% (GLM-5), 92.0% (GPT-5.2-Chat) and 84.4% (GPT-OSS-120B) of failed games.
limits: WordNet taxonomy rules; each model plays both roles; one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Revision needs a test that can refute. S5 should pick checks designed to falsify the current best, which also yields usable entrenchment scores.

source: Ji et al. (2026) ClawArena: AI agents in evolving information environments
finding: Agent benchmark with conflicting sources and staged updates. Revision difficulty depends on the kind of update, not the number: updates that extend earlier evidence are handled; updates that force re-reading earlier claims are not.
numbers: 12 scenarios, 337 rounds, 45 dynamic updates, 5 frameworks, 18 models. Model choice spans a 29-point range in reliability score, framework up to 24 points. The hardest scenario keeps every configuration below 30%.
limits: Authors' own benchmark and score; the MetaClaw skill overlay raises consistency, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Plan for 're-interpretation' updates as the failure class and test S5 on those first.

source: Abtahi et al. (2026) MEDLEY-BENCH: metacognition and belief revision under social pressure
finding: Compares private self-review with revision after other models' outputs. In 30 of 35 models the evaluation-linked component scored lowest relative to the others. Some models shifted strongly when consensus labels were inverted, others near zero.
numbers: 35 models, 12 families, 130 instances. Adversarial subset of 11 models: Mistral Small 3.1 shift +11.6, Qwen3 8B +7.3, others near zero. Human rubric agreement kappa = 0.389 on 24 items.
limits: Authors call it a proof of concept (v1.5 will rerun it); pattern depends on rubric and centring; judge severity not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Models differ widely in how far a fake consensus moves them; do not let S5 treat a vote of other model outputs as evidence.

source: Wang and Koch (2026) Beyond sycophancy: structured resistance and compliance in LLM moral reasoning
finding: Across three studies and eight models, how far a model revises depends on the distance from its own view, who the view is attributed to, and how many peers back it. Models move toward near views and not far ones.
numbers: Sonnet 4.5: probability of moving toward the opposing view is exactly zero across 157 trials at distances 4 to 6 on the scale. Models are more moved by views shown as their own earlier judgments.
limits: Moral dilemmas on Likert scales, not factual claims; only the first page and parts of the results were read.
agent_relevance: Cue source and distance change revision; label the source of each check result so provenance, not tone, sets its weight.

source: Singh (2026) When does belief-based agent memory help? Reliability-conditional updating (Nous)
finding: A Bayesian per-fact belief memory gives no gain over last-write-wins on ordinary conversation memory (LoCoMo subset) because contradictions are rare. It pays off on a benchmark with contradictions and stale facts when source reliability is estimated.
numbers: Contradiction/staleness benchmark of 60 scenarios: belief update 100 vs last-write-wins 67 vs LLM over raw memory 90. Two judges on identical LoCoMo outputs gave 59.97 vs 32.45.
limits: Single-author preprint, own benchmark, 3-conversation subset; reliability estimated from hedging words.
agent_relevance: Simple 'newest wins' is enough when updates do not conflict; add reliability weights only where checks disagree.
